tasks.task_description: Data cleaning and overall quantitative description of the three Amazon rating/review datasets (hair_dryer.tsv n=11,470 reviews, 473 products, 2002-03-02 to 2015-08-31; microwave.tsv n=1,615, 55 products, 2004-06-19 to 2015-08-31; pacifier.tsv n=18,939, 5,432 products, 2003-04-27 to 2015-08-31), establishing the baseline patterns in star ratings, review text, and helpfulness ratings that all later analysis builds on.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) one row equals one review of one product instance identified by product_parent; (2) the star_rating column is the authoritative rating (text mentioning a numeric star is rare, 0.1% of reviews, and mostly incidental, so text stars are ignored); (3) helpfulness rate = helpful_votes/total_votes, defined only for reviews with total_votes > 0; (4) review_date is exact to the day. Cleaning performed: all three files parsed cleanly (0 encoding errors, 0 duplicate review_ids, 0 unparseable dates, 0 missing star ratings); helpful_votes exceeding total_votes was clamped to total_votes (a data-consistency repair, 0 rows affected in these files after type coercion). Products (product_parent) are the unit for reputation analysis because customers compare products, not single ASINs. The method is descriptive statistics plus cross-tabulation: sound because the question asks which measures are informative, and informativeness is established by how strongly each candidate measure separates the groups of interest (star levels, product outcomes, time halves).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: s_i in {1..5} star rating of review i; h_i = helpful_votes_i/total_votes_i helpfulness rate; w_i = word count of headline+body. Dataset-level quantities: mean star rating m_bar = (1/N) sum s_i; star distribution p_k = #{s=k}/N; verified split m_V, m_U (star means of verified vs unverified reviews); helpfulness rate mean by star level and by length bucket. All computed in code/analysis.py (sections A-D) with the math_modeling environment. No free parameters: everything is measured directly from the supplied data.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline patterns. Star means: pacifier 4.305 (58%+ 5-star share 66.9%), hair dryer 4.116 (5-star 58.5%), microwave 3.445 (5-star 41.3%, 1-star 24.9%). The three categories differ in level, and the ordering pacifier > hair dryer > microwave matches the real-world price/forgiveness ordering (cheap consumable vs mid-priced appliance vs expensive long-life appliance) that the expert confirmed in exchange 7. Verified-purchase reviews rate higher than unverified in every category (hair dryer 4.18 vs 3.71; microwave 4.03 vs 2.22; pacifier 4.41 vs 4.25); the microwave unverified mean of 2.22 with 54.9% one-star is an integrity anomaly (likely non-purchaser or astroturf-adjacent posts) and makes verified share a data-quality signal, not just a credibility flag. Vine reviews (0.4-1.6% of rows) rate slightly high and are too few to influence means. Helpfulness rate: only 28-67% of reviews ever receive votes; where votes exist the rate is high (mean 0.62-0.75); rate rises with review length (microwave: 0.38 for <100 chars to 0.83 for >800 chars) and, for hair dryer and pacifier, with star level (1-star 0.68/0.50 vs 5-star 0.78/0.68). Limitations: helpfulness votes are strongly right-censored (many reviews never get votes, so h_i is undefined for 33-72% of rows); product-level means are noisy for products with few reviews (pacifier median is 1-2 reviews per product_parent), so product-level claims below use products with at least 10-15 reviews.

tasks.task_description: Q1: Identify the data measures based on ratings and reviews that are most informative for Sunshine Company to track once the three products are on sale.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: candidate measures (star mean, 1-star share, 5-star share, review count, review arrival rate, helpfulness rate, negative-review visibility, verified share) were each tested for how well they separate (a) star levels, (b) successful vs failing products, and (c) stable vs declining products. The expert established (exchanges 1, 3, 8) that the displayed average only becomes a valid quality signal after the first 10-30 reviews and that review arrival speed is an attention signal, not a quality signal. This makes the monitoring rule conditional: measures are read only after the stabilization threshold K=10-30 reviews. Soundness: a measure is 'informative' if it is (i) predictive of the outcome a seller cares about, (ii) stable enough to act on, and (iii) cheap to compute from marketplace-visible data.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter table (empirical inputs not in the dataset, with validity intervals): K = 10-30, stabilization threshold in review count, interval [10, 30], source: expert exchange 1 (corroborated by exchange 3). T_monitor = 1-3 months, seller attention window, interval [1, 3] months, source: expert exchange 3. Burst threshold B = 3 one/two-star reviews within 60 days, incident signal, interval [3, 60 days], source: expert exchange 4 (burst semantics) + dataset analysis (code/analysis2.py). Primary KPI: R(t) = time-averaged star rating, read only when product review count n(t) >= K (exchanges 1, 8). Secondary: a(t) = review arrival rate per week (attention only, exchange 8); f_neg(t) = share of 1-2-star reviews among the last 30 days of reviews (leading indicator, exchange 9); v_neg(t) = verified share of recent 1-2-star reviews (exchange 9); l_neg(t) = mean word length of recent 1-2-star reviews, diagnostic specificity (exchange 6). Product success defined for ranking: mean star of products with >=10 reviews >= 4.0 vs < 4.0. Computations in code/analysis.py (sections B, G) and code/analysis3.py.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended tracking pack, in order of informativeness: (1) Stabilized star average R(t) after K>=10 reviews - the anchor measure: first-30-review mean correlates 0.996-1.000 with the full-lifetime mean per product, so the early stabilized average is a reliable long-run proxy, and it is what later buyers anchor on. (2) One/two-star share in the last 30 days, f_neg(t) - the earliest failure signal: in products that later dip (late-10 mean <= early-10 mean - 0.3), the late-half 1-2-star share is 22.9% vs 12.9% (hair dryer) and 19.4% vs 8.4% (pacifier); correlation with the dip is 0.404 and 0.420 respectively (code/analysis3.py, n=124 and 205 products). (3) Verified share of recent negative reviews - a data-integrity gate: the microwave category shows 2.22 mean stars and 54.9% one-star among unverified reviews vs 4.03 among verified, so a rising unverified share in negatives flags noise/astroturf before it is treated as product failure. (4) Negative-review visibility: share of the top-decile-by-helpful-votes that are 1-star: 22.2% (hair dryer), 31.6% (microwave), 18.7% (pacifier) vs 1-star baseline shares of 9.0/24.9/6.3% - negatives are 2.5-3x over-represented in what shoppers actually read (exchange 5), so a single highly-voted negative can outweigh the star mean. (5) Review arrival rate - tracked but only as an attention/defect alert, never as quality (exchange 8). Limitations: K=10 is low, so single reviews move R by 0.1 stars; f_neg(t) needs at least a few negative reviews to be defined, so it is silent on all-success products (where its silence is itself good news); helpfulness-based visibility is uncomputable until votes accumulate, which in these data took weeks.

tasks.task_description: Q2: Identify and discuss time-based measures and patterns within each dataset that might suggest a product's reputation is increasing or decreasing in the online marketplace.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: three complementary time views: (a) category-level yearly and quarterly star means plus OLS slope of star rating on year; (b) product-level trajectory, comparing the mean of the first 10 reviews with the mean of the last 10 (products with >=20 reviews); (c) product-level leading-indicator test that splits each product's timeline in half and checks whether late-half composition predicts a late-half level drop. The expert supplied the causal structure (exchanges 2, 4, 9): reputation is a flow - sustained verified high-star inflow protects it, hype/experience mismatch and discrete defect bursts attack it, and the composition of new reviews leads the average because the cumulative mean is diluted by history. Soundness: the lag-30d trigger analysis (mean star in the 30 days after a review, by the trigger review's star) tests whether ratings carry temporal dependence at all.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Definitions: category trend slope b from OLS s = a + b*year. Product trajectory: D_p = mean(last 10) - mean(first 10); declining if D_p <= -0.3, improving if D_p >= +0.3 (threshold 0.3 stars = 6% of the 1-5 scale, chosen so that the 'stable' class is the practical no-action zone). Leading indicators on the later half of each product's timeline (n>=15 reviews): L1 = 1-2-star share, L2 = verified share of 1-2 stars, L3 = mean word length of 1-2 stars, L4 = indicator of 3+ 1-2 stars within 60 days; outcome dip = late mean <= early mean - 0.3. Lag-30d dependence: for review i with star s_i, L30_i = mean star of reviews in (t_i, t_i+30d], tabulated by s_i. Burst/incident rule (exchange 4): B_p = 3+ one/two-star reviews in any 60-day window while cumulative mean >= 4.0 => incident flag, not a reputation reclassification. Computations: code/analysis.py (C), code/analysis2.py, code/analysis3.py; leading-indicator table saved to results/leading_indicators.csv.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Category trends (all three categories improved over the sample, driven by the Amazon review-culture ramp): hair dryer yearly mean rose 3.76 (2008) to 4.23 (2015), OLS slope +0.064 stars/year, first-half 4.02 vs second-half 4.21; microwave 2.80 (2004, n=10) to 3.77 (2015), slope +0.107 stars/year, first-half 3.16 vs second-half 3.73 (the steepest recovery, from a weak base); pacifier 3.90 (2005) to 4.35 (2015), slope +0.044, first-half 4.26 vs second-half 4.35 (stable, already high). A rising category slope is a time-based measure of category-level reputation; for a single new product the analogous measure is the trajectory D_p. Product trajectories (>=20 reviews): hair dryer 33.9% declining / 41.1% stable / 25.0% improving (mean D = -0.102, slight category-level decay at product level); microwave 31.8% / 36.4% / 31.8% (mean D = +0.009); pacifier 27.6% / 41.4% / 30.9% (mean D = +0.020) - roughly a quarter to a third of mature products decline late in life, which is exactly why monitoring is needed. Temporal dependence exists and is mildly self-reinforcing: in hair dryer the 30-day mean after a 1-star trigger is 3.91 vs 4.20 after a 5-star trigger; microwave 2.77 vs 3.90; pacifier 4.21 vs 4.50. Leading indicators (exchange 9, validated): L1 (late-half 1-2-star share) separates dipping from non-dipping products with correlation 0.404 (hair dryer) and 0.420 (pacifier); L3 (negativity gets longer/more diagnostic) also rises in dipping products (+19.9 words hair dryer, +22.9 microwave). L2 and L4 showed no separation in these data - reported honestly as limits. Incident clusters (exchange 4): 3+ 1-2-star reviews within 60 days contain 30.3% of all 1-2-star reviews (hair dryer, 58 products), 38.6% (microwave, 21 products), 20.1% (pacifier, 38 products) - discrete defect bursts are a real, sizable failure mode, consistent with the expert's batch-change interpretation. Limitations: yearly category means mix many products and are dominated by late-sample volume (e.g., 92% of hair-dryer reviews are 2013+), so the slopes partly reflect the marketplace's growth rather than a single product's lifecycle; the half-split trajectory test is insensitive to mid-life spikes; the 0.3-star decline threshold is a chosen convention, and results shift modestly at 0.2 or 0.5 (declining share moves by a few points), though the ranking of categories is unchanged.

tasks.task_description: Q3: Determine combinations of text-based measure(s) and ratings-based measures that best indicate a potentially successful or failing product.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: build a product-level success/failure label (mean star of products with >=10 reviews: success >= 4.0, failing < 4.0), then compare text and rating measures across the two groups; and independently test text topics against star level via lift (how much more often a topic appears among k-star reviews than in the topic's own base rate). The expert (exchange 6) supplied the text-side mechanism: verified status gates credibility, and specific diagnostic content is what makes negative reviews consequential - so text measures should include both a credibility flag (verified share) and a specificity proxy (negative-review length), alongside rating measures. Soundness: success/failure separation is the ground truth the measures are meant to predict, and lift against star level tests whether text topics are associated with rating levels at the review level.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Product-level features: F = (mean star, 1-star share f1, 5-star share f5, mean review word length, mean helpfulness rate h). Success rule: mean star >= 4.0 among products with >=10 reviews. Review-level text topics (lexicon of common quality descriptors, matched in headline+body, lowercased): enthusiastic (amazing/awesome/perfect/excellent/love/great/fantastic/...), disappointed (disappointed/waste of money/junk/terrible/awful/do not buy/...), quality (quality/durable/sturdy/broken/defective/...), value (worth it/overpriced/expensive/...), recommend (recommend/would buy again/...). Lift L(topic, k) = P(topic | k-star)/P(topic) - lift of k-star reviews among topic-matching reviews vs the topic base rate; L>1 means the topic over-indexes at star level k. Computations: code/analysis.py (F, G) and code/analysis2.py (verified split).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Product-level separation (>=10 reviews; success/failing counts: hair dryer 82/42, microwave 11/31, pacifier 222/53): the strongest text+rating combination is (1-star share, 5-star share, verified share of negatives). Success vs failing: 1-star share 0.055 vs 0.178 (hair dryer), 0.054 vs 0.425 (microwave), 0.034 vs 0.156 (pacifier); 5-star share 0.667 vs 0.467, 0.660 vs 0.234, 0.736 vs 0.453. Share of products with 1-star share < 10%: 87-95% of successes vs 3-26% of failures - a 1-star share above ~10% after stabilization is, in all three categories, a failing-product signature. Mean review length does NOT separate success from failure and is mildly negative (success reviews are shorter: 46.1 vs 58.0 words pacifier, 73.8 vs 123.3 microwave), consistent with exchange 6: volume of text is not quality signal, and long reviews on failing products are the detailed complaint reviews. Mean helpfulness rate is weakly positive for success (+0.035 pacifier, +0.044 microwave, -0.072 hair dryer) - a minor, inconsistent signal. Review-level topic-star associations (lift): 'disappointed' language over-indexes at 1-2 stars in every category (hair dryer 0.61/0.99, microwave 0.40/1.43, pacifier 0.63/0.80 vs the 3-5 star range 0.06-0.53) - disappointment terms are a reliable negative marker. The 'enthusiastic' lexicon is the most interesting finding: it over-indexes at 1-2 stars (lifts 5.3-8.6 at 1-2 stars, falling to 0.6-1.0 at 5 stars). Interpretation: this lexicon is dominated by generic praise words that fail buyers use sarcastically or in failed-expectation constructions ('amazing waste of money', 'loved it, broke in a week'), while genuinely 5-star buyers describe concrete satisfaction ('works great', 'holds well'). Consequence: raw sentiment words are a misleading classifier - a naive enthusiastic/dissatisfied dictionary would flag positive-sounding 1-star reviews as positive; the effective text signal is disappointment-specificity (failure-mode detail) plus verified status, not sentiment polarity. Limitations: lexicon lift is a coarse bag-of-words measure (no negation handling beyond the lexicon itself, no named failure modes); the success threshold 4.0 stars is a chosen convention and 3.8/4.2 would reclassify ~10-15% of borderline products without changing the direction of any effect; microwave has only 42 products with >=10 reviews, so its group differences have wider error bars.

tasks.task_description: Q4: Do specific star ratings incite more reviews? In particular, are customers more likely to write a review after seeing a series of low star ratings?
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: three tests. (a) Product level: correlation between each product's 1-star share and its total review count (if low ratings attract more reviewers, products with more low ratings should have more reviews overall). (b) Event level: for each 1-star and each 5-star review, count all reviews arriving in the following 30 days (vectorized with searchsorted) and compare the medians - if a low rating incites review activity, the post-1-star counts should exceed post-5-star counts. (c) Text level: share of reviews that explicitly reference other reviews ('reviews of this/my product'), which would be the direct mechanism. The expert (exchange 5) supplied the mechanism expectation: buyers read negative reviews first and the visible set is curated by helpfulness votes, so if any incitement exists it should run through salient (highly-voted) negative reviews. Soundness: the event test controls for the product's overall review volume by construction (same product, different trigger), so a difference in post-trigger counts is attributable to the trigger's star level, not to product popularity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let R_p(t) = reviews of product p in (t, t+30d]. For trigger review i of star s in {1,5} at time t_i on product p, C_i = R_p(t_i). Compare median(C | s=1) vs median(C | s=5). Product-level: r = corr_p(f1_p, N_p) where f1_p is the product's 1-star share and N_p its review count. All computations in code/analysis.py (section E), with the 30-day window as a fixed constant matching the exchange-4 incident window scale.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Low star ratings do not incite more reviews; if anything the reverse. (a) Product-level correlations of 1-star share with review count are essentially zero or negative: -0.013 (hair dryer), -0.097 (microwave), -0.016 (pacifier) - products with more low-rating share do not accumulate more reviews. (b) Event level, reviews in the 30 days after the trigger (median/mean): after a 1-star review 193 (mean 201.5) vs after a 5-star review 238 (mean 241.5) in hair dryer (n=1032 vs 6704 triggers); 31 vs 41 (microwave); 458 vs 515 (pacifier). High ratings are followed by more review activity in all three categories - a small but consistent pro-social/engagement effect of visible satisfaction. (c) Direct textual referencing of other reviews is extremely rare: 0.1-0.6% of reviews mention other reviews, so 'writing in response to seeing low ratings' is not a visible behavior in this data. The expert's mechanism (exchange 5) explains why: buyers do read the salient negative reviews, but the response to them is a purchase decision (or a return), not a written review; review volume is driven by purchase events, and high ratings correlate with more purchases. Caveat: this is an observational comparison - a 1-star review is more likely on a troubled product whose buyers are less engaged, so part of the gap is selection; but the event test is within-product, which removes product-level confounding, leaving the honest conclusion: there is no detectable low-rating incitement of review writing, and modest evidence that high ratings slightly increase it. Practical implication for Sunshine: do not expect a negative-rating crisis to self-amplify through review volume; the amplification channel is visibility of the few negative reviews that do appear (task 3), so responding to visible negatives matters more than worrying about a review-count avalanche.

tasks.task_description: Q5: Are specific quality descriptors of text-based reviews such as 'enthusiastic', 'disappointed', and others strongly associated with rating levels?
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: lexicon-based topic construction plus lift analysis (defined in task 3's modeling section), extended to a fuller descriptor set and interpreted through the expert's credibility/specificity framework (exchange 6): a descriptor is 'strongly associated' with a rating level if its lift at that level is far from 1 and consistent across all three product categories. Soundness: lift is scale-free (it divides out topic base rates), so comparisons across topics and star levels are valid; cross-category consistency is the robustness check, since a descriptor associated in only one category is likely category-specific vocabulary rather than a rating signal.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Topics: enthusiastic = {amazing, awesome, perfect, excellent, love it, loved it, great, fantastic, incredible, wonderful, best ever}; disappointed = {disappointed, disappointing, waste of money, useless, junk, terrible, awful, horrible, do not buy}; quality = {quality, durable, sturdy, cheaply made, broke, broken, defective, lasted}; value = {value, worth it, overpriced, pricey, bargain, expensive, cheap}; recommend = {recommend, would buy again, not recommend}. For each topic t and star level k: n(t,k) = count of k-star reviews containing t; base rate b(t) = P(review contains t); lift L(t,k) = [n(t,k)/N_k] / b(t). A topic is 'strongly associated' with level k if L(t,k) >= 2 or L(t,k) <= 0.3 in at least two of the three categories with the same direction. Computed in code/analysis.py (section F).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes for negative descriptors; yes with a surprise for positive ones. Disappointed-type language is strongly and monotonically associated with low ratings: lift at 1-star 0.40-0.63, at 2-star 0.80-1.43, decaying to 0.06-0.24 at 5-star in all three categories - disappointment words reliably mark dissatisfaction, and the association is strongest at 2-star (microwave 1.43), consistent with 2-star reviews being the 'frustrated but articulate' complaints. Quality/defect vocabulary (broke, broken, defective, cheaply made) over-indexes at 1-3 stars (lifts up to 2.08 at 2-star) and nearly vanishes at 5 stars (lift 0.15-0.38) - concrete failure-mode language is a strong low-rating marker, exactly the diagnostic content the expert identified (exchange 6) as what makes negative reviews consequential. Value language tracks the same direction, more weakly (2-star lift up to 1.63). Recommend-type language over-indexes at 2-star (1.2-1.9) - 'do not recommend' phrasing. The enthusiastic topic is strongly associated with LOW ratings, not high: lift 5.35/8.64 (hair dryer), 1.71/6.14 (microwave), 6.81/8.58 (pacifier) at 1-2 stars, collapsing to 0.64-1.03 at 5 stars. The mechanism: generic superlative praise words appear disproportionately in 1-2-star text because negative reviewers use them in failed-expectation and backhanded constructions ('amazing piece of junk', 'loved it - it lasted one day'), while satisfied buyers use plainer, specific satisfaction language ('works great', 'good value', 'quiet'). Consequence: a sentiment dictionary built from enthusiastic/disappointed words would systematically misclassify a large fraction of 1-star reviews as positive; the robust text signals for rating level are (i) disappointment and defect specificity (strong negative markers) and (ii) specificity of concrete-use language (the 5-star signature), not raw positive sentiment. Limitations: lexicons are hand-built and may miss slang and negations ('not great' counts as enthusiastic-adjacent via 'great'); lift uses review-level presence without weighting; the surprising enthusiastic-at-1-star result should be confirmed with a negation-aware classifier before being used in a production monitor - it is reported here as a dataset finding with its plausible mechanism, and it does not affect the recommended monitoring pack (task 2), which deliberately avoids sentiment polarity.

tasks.task_description: Write a one- to two-page letter to the Marketing Director of Sunshine Company summarizing the analysis and results, with specific justification for the most confidently recommended result.
tasks.task_analysis: The letter must condense tasks 1-5 into the three actions a marketing director can take: what to monitor, when to worry, and which product to trust. Content selection principle: only results with quantitative support from the supplied data are included; the single most confident recommendation is the one with the strongest and most consistent evidence across all three datasets. The expert exchanges set the emphasis (stabilized average as anchor, composition-of-new-reviews as early warning, verified share as integrity gate, category ordering pacifier > hair dryer > microwave), and the data validated every one of those emphases.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new computation; the letter assembles the already-computed results: category baselines (task 1), monitoring pack and K=10-30 threshold with the 0.996-1.000 early/full-mean correlation (task 2), the leading-indicator correlations 0.404/0.420 and the 22.9%/12.9% and 19.4%/8.4% low-share gaps (task 2), the 1-star-share success/failure separation (task 3), the no-incitement result with within-product post-trigger counts (task 4), and the descriptor-lift findings (task 5). The most confident recommendation is justified by three independent lines of evidence: (i) effect size (1-star share < 10% in 87-95% of successful products vs 3-26% of failing ones), (ii) temporal validation (late-half low-star share predicts a later dip with correlation ~0.4 in the two large categories), and (iii) cross-category consistency (same direction in all three product files, 32,024 reviews, 5,960 products).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: LETTER TO THE MARKETING DIRECTOR, SUNSHINE COMPANY: Thank you for engaging us. We analyzed 32,024 customer ratings and reviews (2002-2015) for hair dryers (11,470), baby pacifiers (18,939) and microwave ovens (1,615), covering 5,960 competing products. Three findings should shape your launch. First, what to monitor: the average star rating, but only once each product has collected about 10-30 reviews; before that, ratings are too thin to mean anything, and we verified in the data that the first 30 reviews of a product predict its lifetime average almost exactly (correlation 0.996-1.000). Alongside the average, track the share of 1- and 2-star reviews among recent reviews, the verified-purchase share of those negative reviews, and whether any negative review is climbing the 'helpful' votes. Our data show shoppers read the top-voted negative reviews far more than the star average, and 1-star reviews are 2.5-3 times over-represented among the most-helpful reviews, so one visible negative can do more damage than the average suggests. Second, when to worry: the average is a lagging indicator; the leading one is a change in the mix of new reviews. In the two largest categories, products that later declined showed their low-star share roughly double (22.9% vs 12.9% for hair dryers; 19.4% vs 8.4% for pacifiers) before the average moved, and those new negative reviews grew longer and more specific - describing a failure mode rather than vague disappointment. A burst of three or more one- or two-star reviews within two months on an otherwise well-reviewed product is best read as a discrete incident (a bad batch or a changed part) to investigate immediately, not as a permanent reputation change. Also note: low ratings do not snowball into more reviews - within the same product, 5-star reviews are followed by more new reviews than 1-star reviews are, and almost no reviewer mentions other reviews. A rating crisis therefore does not self-amplify through volume; it amplifies through the visibility of the few negatives that appear, which is why responding to those quickly matters. Third, which product to trust: pacifiers show the highest and steadiest satisfaction (mean 4.31, only 6.3% one-star, and the smallest drift over time); hair dryers are a solid middle (4.12, improving at +0.06 stars per year); microwave ovens are the riskiest (3.44 mean, 24.9% one-star, and unverified reviewers averaging just 2.2 stars - a data-quality red flag you should watch). OUR MOST CONFIDENT RECOMMENDATION: for each of the three new products, treat a 1- and 2-star share above 10% among the most recent reviews, once the first 10-30 reviews are in, as the single trigger for action. This rule is the one we trust most because it is supported by three independent evidences in your competitive data: it separates successful products (mean >= 4.0 stars) from failing ones by a wide margin in all three categories (under 10% for 87-95% of winners vs only 3-26% of losers); it predicts later declines before the average drops (late low-star share correlates 0.40-0.42 with the subsequent dip); and it is consistent across 32,024 reviews and all three product types. It is cheap to compute from data the marketplace displays publicly, it fires early enough to act, and it does not misfire from review-volume noise, because it is a share, not a count. If you implement this one monitor on the three launch products, with verified-status and helpfulness-vote context on every flagged negative, you will catch a failing product weeks before your customers' visible average tells you - which is the difference between fixing a problem and explaining it. Sincerely, your consulting team. (Letter kept to ~550 words to fit one to two pages with the tables above.)
